newsitem.title: UK: Britain's spies told they need commercial help.
newsitem.headline: Britain's spies told they need commercial help.

text.p: Britain's intelligence services, under pressure to prove their worth in the cost-conscious post-Cold War era, should hire outside consultants and spy more on economic targets, intelligence observers said on Monday.

But an academic and a former top intelligence gatherer rejected arguments that Britain could retain its high diplomatic profile if it stopped spying operations and relied instead on commercially gathered and publicly available information.

"Real comparative advantage remains with those nations whose knowledge base outstrips that of the competition," Professor Peter Hennessy told the Royal Institute of International Affairs in a lecture.

"Intelligence, without question, is an influence multiplier." Hennessy was speaking on the day the Security Service Act came into effect, allowing the MI5 intelligence service to fight organised crime alongside British police.

The end of the Cold War has shifted the focus to "second order threats" -- organised crime, terrorism and weapons proliferation -- which are more difficult to justify spending a billion pounds ($1.5 billion) a year to monitor, said Hennessy.
But Michael Herman, a former top civil servant at Britain's main electronic evesdropping centre, said the more diverse range of threats nations face still justified spending large sums.
Intelligence failures illustrate how costly turning a blind eye can be, Herman argues in a book he has just published on the future role of the intelligence services.
He cited Britain's failure to foresee the 1981 Argentinian invasion of the Falklands Islands and Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990 as examples.

Other recommendations to improve the efficiency of the country's network of spies, listening networks and image gatherers include boosting the status of analysts and rethinking Britain's close intelligence ties to the United States.
Some mistakes could have been avoided if the people paid to sift through mountains of data and reports from agents were given greater recognition, Herman said.
"Analysts in the defence intelligence staff were second class citizens during my era," he told Reuters.

Both Herman and Hennessy foresaw Britain gradually cutting its intelligence budget in coming years, and called for consultants to be brought into secretive departments to boost efficiency, as has happened in other government ministries.

Hennessy called for "a more full-hearted approach to economic and industrial intelligence" to make better use of intelligence resources, but did not suggest who should be targeted. Countries like France, the United States and Japan regularly accuse each of other of commercial espionage.

Hennessy added that until there was a thorough review of Britain's shrinking global importance and threats to its intelligence ties with the United States, it would be hard for intelligence planners to cut costs dramatically.
